# AI-First Support

`customer_support.model.ai_first_support` · model · parent `—`

> An automated system answers first and a human is the exception rather than the default. The queue empties, the clock stops mattering, and the entire apparatus this domain built around waiting — first response targets, backlog age, coverage windows, the overnight thin hour — loses most of its force. That is a real gain and it is not the interesting part. . The interesting part is that the failure mode moves. Reactive human support fails by being slow, and slow announces itself: there is a clock, a breach, an ageing ticket and an increasingly annoyed customer, and every one of those is instrumented. This branch fails by being confidently wrong, and wrong is silent. A fluent, plausible, incorrect answer is accepted, acted on, and produces no signal at the moment of failure. The customer does not complain, because they do not yet know. They come back two days later about a different symptom, or they do not come back at all, or — the expensive case — they did what they were told and it destroyed something. . So the branch's central operational question is not "how fast did we answer" but "what happened after we answered", and that is a signal nobody instruments by default. The reopen, the second contact on a new symptom, the escalation immediately following an automated reply: these are the only wrong-answer detectors available without new telemetry, and they are all lagging. Anything that shortens the distance between a wrong answer and the discovery of it is worth more in this branch than anything that improves the answer rate. . Apology economics change with it. "We were slow" is forgivable and routine. "Your system told me to run this" is a different conversation, and in regulated or financial contexts it is a liability event rather than a service one. Confidence calibration therefore stops being a model property and becomes a support policy: what the system is allowed to assert without a citation, and what it must refuse, are decisions with an owner. . Two structural consequences that surprise operators. First, the knowledge base becomes production infrastructure. A stale article was previously a bad page that some customers found; it is now a wrong answer in the company's voice, delivered instantly, at scale, to everyone who asks. Article freshness moves from editorial hygiene to a release dependency. Second, cost stops scaling with volume, and the people who used to notice things leave the queue. When thirty percent of contacts are one defect, that fact used to be discovered by an agent who got bored of typing the same reply. Nobody gets bored now, so the aggregate signal has to be manufactured deliberately or it does not exist. . What an operator carries over wrongly from a human queue: containment rate as a success metric. Containment counts conversations that did not reach a human, and a customer who gave up is contained. Read alone it rewards exactly the behaviour that destroys the branch — making the handoff to a person hard — and it will look excellent right up until the churn cohort lands.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | the same population as whatever motion is being automated, with one difference that matters: they do not know how much the system knows, so they under-specify and then blame themselves for the wrong answer |
| typical_resolution_hours | 1 |
| volume_shape | smooth and volume-insensitive at the automated layer, extremely spiky at the human layer — the humans see only the residue, which is the hard tail plus everyone the system upset |
| staffing_model | a small senior human team behind an automated first line, doing exception handling, quality review of automated answers, and knowledge repair |
| coverage | 24x7 at the automated layer and something much narrower behind it, which is the gap customers discover at 3am |
| automation_level | very high and explicitly so — the branch is defined by the automated layer being the default path rather than a deflection attempt in front of one |
| primary_channels | `chat`, `in_app`, `email`, `help_center` |
| notes | The human team in this branch is doing a harder job than a tier-one agent, not an easier one. Every conversation they receive has already failed once, arrives mid-context, and carries a customer who has spent effort and been let down by something that sounded certain. Staffing it with the juniors freed up by the automation is the most common and most expensive implementation error in the branch.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `accuracy_state`, `last_verified_at`, `verified_against_version`, `intent_covered`


> `verified_against_version` is the attribute that stops being paperwork in this branch. A human agent reading a stale article notices the screenshot is from the old UI; the automated layer does not, and answers anyway. Article freshness is a production dependency here, and an article whose verified version is behind the shipped version should be treated as an outage of that intent rather than as a backlog item.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `reopen_count`, `verified_by_customer`, `resolution_type`


> The reopen is the primary wrong-answer detector and the only one available with no new instrumentation, which is why auto-closing after an automated answer is so damaging: it suppresses the single signal the branch runs on in exchange for a metric. A contact answered automatically and reopened once should be treated as a defect in the answer, not as a customer who did not read it.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.customer_sentiment`

Requires `read_confidence_bp`, `expression_style`, `measured_on`


> A customer who has just been confidently misinformed reads as satisfied. They thank the system and leave. This makes the positive sentiment read immediately following an automated answer the least trustworthy reading anywhere in the library — it is indistinguishable from a correct answer at the moment it is taken, and only the follow-on behaviour separates them. Discount it explicitly rather than treating a thank you as a resolution.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `context_package`, `context_handed_over`, `requested_at`


> A handoff to a human that does not carry the transcript makes the customer repeat everything they already typed, to a person, after being failed by a machine. It is the most reliably enraging sequence in this branch and it is a plumbing problem, not a service one. `requested_at` matters because the interval between the automated answer and the escalation request is itself the cleanest confidence signal available on that answer.
